title: 18 U.S.C. section 2703 — required disclosure under the Stored Communications Act
body: Public edition. Public legal record, fact-checked reference. Section 2703 sets the federal standards for compelling a provider to disclose stored communications and records. Contents in electronic storage generally require a warrant; non-content records may be obtained by subpoena, 2703(d) court order, or warrant. After Carpenter v. United States (2018), seven or more days of historical CSLI requires a warrant supported by probable cause, even though the statute's text permits lesser process for non-content records. The statute remains the starting framework every court applies. title: 18 U.S.C. section 2703(d) — the "specific and articulable facts" court order
body: Public edition. Public legal record, fact-checked reference. A 2703(d) order issues when the government shows "specific and articulable facts showing that there are reasonable grounds to believe" the records sought are relevant and material to an ongoing criminal investigation. This standard sits between a subpoena and probable cause. Post-Carpenter, a 2703(d) order no longer suffices for seven-plus days of historical CSLI, but it remains the standard for shorter CSLI periods and other non-content records in many jurisdictions. title: 18 U.S.C. section 2701 — unlawful access to stored communications
body: Public edition. Public legal record, fact-checked reference. Section 2701 criminalizes intentionally accessing, without authorization, a facility through which an electronic communication service is provided, and thereby obtaining or altering a stored communication. It is the SCA's anti-hacking provision. It frames the private-side boundary: unauthorized acquisition of someone else's stored location records can be a federal crime, distinct from lawful government process under section 2703. title: 18 U.S.C. section 2702 — voluntary disclosure and the emergency exception
body: Public edition. Public legal record, fact-checked reference. Section 2702 generally bars providers from voluntarily disclosing customer communications and records, with exceptions including the subscriber's consent and emergencies. Section 2702(b)(8) and (c)(4) permit emergency disclosure to a governmental entity when the provider, in good faith, believes an emergency involving danger of death or serious physical injury requires disclosure without delay. Carriers publish emergency-request procedures under this provision. title: 18 U.S.C. section 2705 — delayed notice
body: Public edition. Public legal record, fact-checked reference. Delayed-notice orders are a routine companion to CSLI process and are subject to judicial oversight. title: 18 U.S.C. section 2703(f) — preservation of records
body: Public edition. Public legal record, fact-checked reference. Preservation requests are the standard first step before seeking CSLI, ensuring records are not deleted under routine retention schedules while process is prepared. title: 18 U.S.C. sections 3121-3127 — pen registers and trap-and-trace devices
body: Public edition. Public legal record, fact-checked reference. The Pen Register Act governs prospective collection of non-content dialing, routing, addressing, and signaling information, requiring a court order based on certification that the information is relevant to an ongoing criminal investigation. Orders last up to 60 days and may be extended. The Act's framework interacts with CSLI law where prospective location signaling is at issue, though Carpenter-era courts increasingly require warrants for prospective location tracking. title: 18 U.S.C. section 2518 — Title III wiretap orders
body: Public edition. Public legal record, fact-checked reference. Section 2518 sets the "super-warrant" standard for real-time interception of wire, oral, or electronic communications: probable cause plus a showing of necessity (normal investigative procedures have been tried and failed or are too dangerous). Title III governs real-time content interception; location-information collection that amounts to a search under Carpenter and its progeny is analyzed under Fourth Amendment warrant standards rather than Title III's content-interception rules. title: 47 U.S.C. section 1002 — CALEA assistance capability
body: Public edition. Public legal record, fact-checked reference. The statute expressly excludes from "call-identifying information" any information that may disclose the physical location of the subscriber, except as otherwise authorized — a legislative recognition that location data deserves distinct treatment, later vindicated by Carpenter. title: California Penal Code sections 1546-1546.4 — CalECPA (2015)
body: Public edition. Public legal record, fact-checked reference. The California Electronic Communications Privacy Act (2015) requires a warrant or wiretap order for government access to electronic communication information, including location information, with notice to the target and annual reporting by the state Attorney General. CalECPA is the leading enacted state model extending Carpenter-like warrant protection to location records, and several states have since adopted similar CSLI warrant statutes.
